A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MEMENTO study and contain readable main text and Appendices A–F. Text and visual inspection support matching the equations, experiments, figures, tables, and relocated appendix material.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulator experiments on personalized embodied agents, memory-design comparisons, and human-baseline, retrieval, and robustness results in Appendix E.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds long-context QA, task-complexity, and user-profile-memory robustness analyses.

M1.justification: The ReAct planner, episodic memory, hierarchical user-profile graph, and update/retrieval procedures are retained. Appendix D.1 expands the description of node replacement and reuse and renames an algorithm operation; this documents the existing procedure without establishing an actual method change.

E1.justification: v3 adds personalized-knowledge extraction in QA form (D.5) and paraphrased graph-update/node-reference scenarios (E.4.4). These extend task requirements within the existing household setting. The main MEMENTO coverage and earlier multi-memory, ambiguous-instruction, and generalization scenarios remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The same six LLM variants participate in the main and memory-quality comparisons. Memory-format alternatives, human baselines, and similarity, reranking, and query-expansion comparators are retained. The new diagnostics introduce no additional competing method.

E3.justification: The new QA evaluation varies retrieved-memory counts from 1 to 20 and uses GPT-4o to judge answers against gold memories. The graph robustness test uses ten modified instructions per noise type, three annotators, one scene, and graphs initialized from original instructions. These are additional protocols; the principal acquisition/utilization settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds three substantive diagnostics: object-location-count distributions to examine task-complexity confounding (C.3.4), long-context QA to distinguish knowledge recall from planning difficulties (D.5), and graph-update/node-reference robustness with explicit failure cases (E.4.4). Together these substantially broaden analysis of the central bottlenecks and proposed memory module.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same dataset-filtering confidence intervals and Krippendorff's alpha analysis in C.3.2–C.3.3. v3 introduces no additional repeated-run, seed, significance-testing, or uncertainty-reporting practice for its new diagnostics.

E6.justification: Substantial new diagnostic results include QA accuracies (Table 15: at k=20, 95.69% for GPT-4o and 83.19% for Qwen-2.5-72B), graph-noise accuracies (Table 26: 100% for updates and 75% for node references), failure cases, and task-complexity distributions. Table 16 expands v2 Figure 11 with completion and planning-cost results; Qwen-2.5-7B's high-quality joint-memory SR is reported as 8.3%, versus approximately 14% in the earlier plot, without an explained setting change. Figure 7's Llama-3.1-70B annotation changes from -83.3 to -83.4; Tables 1–2 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, goal and trajectory definitions, Equation 1, and mathematical content of the graph algorithms are retained. The revised observation wording and algorithm-operation name do not introduce new assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: MEMENTO's two-stage evaluation, the object-semantics/user-pattern distinction, overload and coordination bottlenecks, and benefits of combining hierarchical user-profile memory with episodic memory. Added appendix evidence supports these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes successful knowledge recall in QA from difficulties applying it during planning, argues that object-location counts do not explain the knowledge-type performance gap, and identifies duplicate graph nodes as a concrete failure mode. E.2.1 also emphasizes memory clarity and planning efficiency. These refine the retained bottleneck interpretation and applicability limits.

D1.justification: D.1 newly explains knowledge-node replacement and similarity-threshold-based reuse of object/location nodes, although the threshold value remains unspecified. Section 3.4 clarifies that acquisition episodes are collected before utilization. v3 also provides the noisy instruction pairs and replaces anonymous code-access information with a stated public GitHub code/data location.

R1.justification: Section 2, Appendix B, and the reference list retain the same cited works and research positioning concerning embodied planning, memory systems, and personalization.

P1.justification: Edits are localized: v3 adds the conference header and acknowledgements, clarifies observation/retrieval wording, expands graph-update explanations, rewrites the memory-quality discussion, and adds appendix subsections. The main narrative and section hierarchy remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Appendix displays are substantially reorganized: v2 Tables 16–21 move from within or after the prompts into D.4 as v3 Tables 9–14, and Figures 12–13 are reformatted and moved beside the graph description. The old memory-quality Figure 11 becomes expanded Table 16. v3 adds a new Figure 11 and QA/noise-analysis tables, alongside resizing and resolution adjustments to main-text plots.

improvement.justification: The added complexity check, QA diagnostic, and graph-noise failure analysis strengthen support for the existing conclusions and clarify their limits. Expanded update documentation and better placement of examples also improve inspectability. The small single-scene robustness test, model-based QA judging, and unexplained memory-quality score revision limit the strength of this gain.
